questions.question: The CSS 'cascade' refers to:

options.text: The algorithm that resolves which declarations apply when multiple rules match

questions.explanation: The cascade combines origin/importance, specificity, and source order to decide the winning value for each property.

questions.question: The cascade resolution order starts with:

options.text: Origin & importance (e.g. user !important vs author vs UA styles)

questions.explanation: Step 1 is origin/importance (user-agent < author < author !important < user !important). Specificity/order come later.

questions.question: User-agent (browser default) styles are overridden by:

options.text: Author stylesheets (your CSS) in normal cases

questions.explanation: Author (website) styles normally beat UA defaults. Resets/normalizers exist precisely to override UA inconsistencies.

questions.question: What does the 'inherit' keyword do for a property?

options.text: Forces the value to be taken from the parent element

questions.explanation: inherit explicitly takes the parent's computed value. Some properties (color, font-family) inherit automatically; others don't.

questions.question: The 'initial' keyword sets a property to:

options.text: Its CSS specification-defined initial value (not the UA style)

questions.explanation: initial resets to the property's defined initial value per spec (e.g. color: initial = black), distinct from the browser default look.

questions.question: Two rules with identical specificity and origin — the winner is decided by:
questions.explanation: After origin/importance and specificity are equal, the cascade falls back to source order: last declaration wins.

questions.question: Why is understanding the cascade important in large apps (e.g. Angular)?

options.text: To predictably override third-party/component styles without !important sprawl
It only matters for print media

questions.explanation: With many layers (libs, components, themes), the cascade explains why a style wins; raise specificity intentionally rather than spray !important.

questions.question: The 'revert' keyword (vs initial/unset) means:

options.text: Roll back to the value the cascade would have had without the current author rule (UA or inherited)

questions.explanation: revert undoes the author-level change, falling back to UA style or inherited value (depending on the property) — smarter than initial.
